Chapter 3: Setting Realistic Goals and Cutting Them in Half
Big dreams are exciting, aren’t they? But let’s be honest—sometimes, those ambitious goals can feel overwhelming. When you set your sights too high or squeeze your timeline too tight, the urge to give up creeps in fast.
So, what’s the answer? You don’t have to let go of your big dreams—just try approaching them in a way that actually makes finishing possible.
Here’s a strategy that might sound a little counterintuitive at first: cut your goals in half.
Wait, cut them in half? Why aim lower when you’re trying to achieve more?
Well, here’s the thing—research and real-world experience show that smaller goals are much more likely to get done. And when you finish something, you build confidence. That confidence? It fuels your next step forward.
Picture this: you want to lose twenty pounds in two months. That’s a tall order. Instead, what if you aimed for ten pounds? It’s still a challenge, but it feels doable. And when you hit that ten-pound mark, you’ll feel accomplished and motivated to keep going. If you’d shot for twenty and missed, you might’ve felt discouraged—and maybe even quit.
This approach works in all kinds of situations. Think about writing a book. Rather than setting a goal for a hundred thousand words, why not start with fifty thousand? Or maybe you’re starting a business. Focus on launching just one product instead of an entire line. Learning a new skill? Try practicing for fifteen minutes a day, instead of a whole hour.
Cutting goals in half doesn’t mean settling for less. It’s about building momentum—a track record of finishing what you start. And once you hit that first, smaller goal, you can always build from there. Suddenly, your journey is a set of manageable steps, not one gigantic leap.
And here’s something else to pay attention to: life’s unpredictable. Obstacles will pop up, no matter how well you plan. That’s why it helps to build some flexibility into your goals. If things don’t go as expected, you’re ready to adapt, instead of getting stuck.
Try thinking of your goals as experiments, not tests. An experiment is a chance to learn and adjust, while a test feels like it’s pass or fail. This way of thinking helps you stay curious and flexible—even when things don’t go perfectly.
So, how can you put all of this into practice?
First, get clear on your original goal and timeline. Then, cut that goal in half to make it more attainable. Break it down into smaller tasks or milestones, so each step feels doable. Track your progress, and celebrate every win—no matter how small. And if you hit a bump, adjust your plan, and treat setbacks as information, not failure.
By setting goals that are realistic—and cutting them in half—you’ll find the path to finishing is a lot clearer and way less intimidating. You’ll shift your focus from huge ambitions to steady progress. And that’s how you build the habit of getting things done.
This approach sets you up for the next challenge: handling those hidden obstacles that can throw even the best plans off track.
